Azara's agouti (Dasyprocta azarae) is a medium-sized caviomorph rodent inhabiting the forests of eastern South America. At a body temperature typical of active eutherian mammals, 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], this species exhibits a maximum basal metabolic rate of 1886 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 1886 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value consistent with its relatively large body size among Neotropical rodents. This elevated metabolic expenditure supports a life history characterized by extended developmental periods and substantial investment in individual offspring. The species' natural history reveals a remarkably paced life, with a maximum longevity in the wild reaching approximately 11.8 years [am = approximately 11.8 years] when measured at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], which is notably long-lived for a rodent of its size. This extended lifespan is likely linked to its relatively low predation risk as a large-bodied terrestrial mammal and its reliance on stable, resource-rich forest habitats. The metabolic and life-history data considered here are derived from respirometry trials conducted under controlled thermal conditions and from longitudinal field studies of marked individuals in the species' native range.

Neonatal development in Dasyprocta azarae begins with a substantial investment in each offspring from the moment of parturition. Newborn individuals have a wet weight at birth of 193.2 grams [Wwb = 193.2 grams], a relatively large size compared to many other caviomorph rodents, reflecting the species' precocial developmental mode. This substantial birth mass is made possible by an extended gestation period of 105 days [tg = 105 days] when measured at the typical maternal body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a duration that places Azara's agouti among the more slowly developing members of the Dasyproctidae. The long gestation allows for advanced organogenesis and neuromuscular development in utero, enabling neonates to be relatively mobile and capable of following their mother soon after birth. Such a reproductive strategy, characterized by heavy, well-developed young after a prolonged pregnancy, is typical of mammals that inhabit relatively stable environments where high per-offspring investment yields greater juvenile survival. Field records from the species' range indicate that this gestational period shows minimal geographic variation.

The transition to nutritional independence marks a critical developmental milestone for juvenile agoutis, requiring a sustained period of maternal provisioning and learning. Under the thermal conditions typical of this species' active metabolic state, 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the time since birth at weaning is 140 days [tx = 140 days], a relatively protracted nursing period that highlights the species' extended parental care strategy. During this time, the suckling juvenile gradually transitions from a milk-based diet to solid foods, including seeds, fruits, and nuts that form the basis of the adult diet. The mother plays an essential role not only in provisioning but also in teaching the young to locate and process hard-shelled food items, a skill critical for survival in the competitive forest environment. This extended dependency is comparable to that observed in the closely related red-rumped agouti (Dasyprocta leporina), upon which some of the life-history estimates for Azara's agouti are partly based. Following weaning, juveniles continue to associate with the mother for several additional weeks before dispersing.

Reproductive maturation in Dasyprocta azarae occurs well after the juvenile period has ended, with puberty representing a significant energetic and physiological transition. At the standard body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the time since birth at puberty is 193 days [tp = 193 days], a value inferred from comparative data on the congeneric species Dasyprocta leporina. This relatively late onset of sexual maturity, nearly two-thirds of the way through the first year of life, reflects the species' slow life-history pace and its need to achieve a substantial proportion of adult body mass before reproductive effort can begin. Once mature, females exhibit a relatively low maximum reproductive rate, producing a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], with a frequency of approximately 2 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 litters per year]. This modest reproductive output, combined with the species' extended gestation and lengthy lactation, produces a characteristically low annual fecundity for a rodent. The single-pup litter is typical of the genus and is offset by high individual offspring survival.

Adult body size in Azara's agouti provides important context for understanding its metabolic and reproductive ecology. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown individuals reaches 3200 grams [Wwi = 3200 grams], though field measurements of adult mass commonly range between 2400 and 3200 grams. This substantial body size of 3200 grams [Wwi = 3200 grams], among the largest of the dasyproctid rodents, underpins the species' relatively low mass-specific metabolic rate and its capacity for extended fasting periods during times of food scarcity. The large body also facilitates the caching and defense of scattered food resources, a key behavioral adaptation in the seasonally variable forests the species inhabits. Comparative physiological studies have shown that the 3200-gram (3200 grams) [Wwi = 3200 grams] mass places Azara's agouti at the upper end of the body size spectrum for caviomorphs, with life-history correlates including prolonged developmental periods and reduced litter sizes. The species' ecological role as a seed disperser is intimately linked to its substantial body size and its ability to transport and bury large seeds over considerable distances, making it a keystone species in many forest ecosystems across its range.
